description: The Average Lies, a fact-checking tool that tests climate claims from the news against 25 years of NASA Earth data across 360 two-degree study areas. Regional averages often hide growing swings between wet and dry months or opposing trends in neighbouring areas. Our tool tests each claim for trends in both the average and the monthly swings using seasonal linear models in Python, then maps the results and reports the statistical confidence of every verdict in a Vite and d3-geo web interface.
summary: he Average Lies is a fact-checking intelligence tool built for the Earth System Trend Detective challenge. It tests climate claims from the news against 25 years of NASA Earth data, place by place, and states how confident each answer is. Climate claims in public reporting are rarely checked against measurements. When they are checked, a regional average often hides local reality: an average can stay flat while the swings between wet and dry months grow, and neighbouring areas can trend in opposite directions. We combined monthly observations from NASA POWER, MERRA-2, GPM IMERG and GLDAS Noah 2.1 across 10 environmental records and 360 two-degree study areas from January 2000 to December 2024. Users can paste news text into a Claims Desk to receive statistical verdicts, search across variables and multi-condition filters in a Survey tool, or inspect an Index Globe and regional Place Plates. The tool gives journalists, students and the public a direct way to test claims and see where trends hold.
details:
THE PROBLEM Climate claims in the news, such as "Somalia is drying" or "rain in Balochistan is getting more erratic", are rarely checked against satellite and model measurements. Where they are checked, a regional average often hides what is happening on the ground. An average can stay flat while the swings between wet and dry months grow. Two neighbouring areas can also trend in opposite directions. Journalists, students and the public have no quick way to test a claim, see where it holds and where it does not, and know how sure the answer is.

WHAT THE PRODUCT DOES

  1. Claims Desk: Users paste a sentence, a paragraph or a whole article. Each sentence that names a place, a measure and a direction is tested. Each claim is shown on an evidence board that connects the claim to the place, measure and direction it was tested as, then to every study area it covers, the two statistical tests, and a verdict (Backed, Partly backed, Opposite, Partly opposite, Depends where, Not shown). Sentences that cannot be tested are listed with the reason. The board exports as a report.
  2. Survey: A pattern-search tool. Users ask for areas where a measure's average or swings changed, combine two conditions (for example rain swings growing and topsoil getting drier), limit by country or region, and rank by confidence or size of change. Results show on a map, a scatter chart plotting change in average against change in swings, a ranked table, and a side-by-side comparison. Results export as CSV and GeoJSON.
  3. Index Globe: A printed-atlas globe with numbered markers for the key findings and an index explaining each one.
  4. Place Plates: A full page per study area with its monthly record, the trend in the average, the trend in the swings, a second NASA record where one exists, and the nearest area moving the other way.
  5. Guided Tour and Method: A guided walkthrough of three primary findings alongside full methodological documentation.

DATA AND METHOD We analysed 360 study areas, each 2° by 2° (about 220 km across), using monthly observations from January 2000 to December 2024 across 10 NASA records:

  • NASA POWER (from MERRA-2): air temperature (T2M), relative humidity (RH2M), corrected rainfall (PRECTOTCORR), and topsoil wetness (GWETTOP).
  • MERRA-2 aerosol: aerosol optical depth (haze) and dust.
  • GPM IMERG: satellite rainfall.
  • GLDAS Noah 2.1: evaporation, surface runoff, and soil moisture.

Our statistical pipeline applies five steps in Python:

  • Seasons removed: each month is compared only with the same calendar month in other years.
  • Average test: a seasonal linear trend using ordinary least squares with Newey-West (HAC, 12-month) standard errors, which allow for runs of similar months.
  • Swings test: the trend in the size of each month's departure from normal, after removing the season and the long-term trend.
  • Rare-month check: the share of recent months above the old 90th percentile.
  • Multiple testing: 3,545 trend tests corrected together with Benjamini-Hochberg, so fewer than 1 in 20 passing results should be chance.

For a second opinion, rain is measured by MERRA-2 and GPM, and soil is measured by MERRA-2 and GLDAS. Where they disagree, both are reported. Records sensitive to the 2013-15 satellite changeover (temperature, aerosol, dust, GPM rain) are kept out of the headline counts. Early-warning signals of tipping points and natural clusters of places were also tested; neither survived correction and they are not shown. Claims are read with a fixed vocabulary of places, measures and directions. No AI writes any verdict or answer.

VERIFIED FINDINGS

  • 39 areas show growing swings while the average shows no significant change.
  • 17 pairs of neighbouring areas (under 700 km apart) trend in opposite directions, covering 25 areas.
  • 23 places show disagreement between two NASA systems (3 for rain, 20 for soil).
  • In MERRA-2 rain records, 83 areas are significantly wetter, 27 are drier, and 33 have growing swings.
  • Pasni, Pakistan: average rain shows no significant change (q = 0.07). Swings are up 51% a decade (q = 0.028). A month that was a 1-in-10 event now comes about 1 in 3. July 2022 recorded 7.1 mm a day against a July normal of 0.8.
  • Lodwar, Turkana, Kenya: runoff swings are up 31% a decade (q = 0.003), and satellite rain swings are up 18%.
  • Somalia: Iskushuban and Burao, about 530 km apart, have significant topsoil trends in opposite directions.
  • Western Sahel, Niger: MERRA-2 topsoil is wetter (q = 0.0008), while GLDAS soil is drier (q = 0.0004).

CLAIMS CHECKED FROM REAL REPORTING

  • Dawn (7 Jul 2022) claim: "Rain in Balochistan is getting more erratic" -> Verdict: Backed.
  • REACH (2023) claim: "Floods in Turkana are getting more extreme" -> Verdict: Backed.
  • The National, on World Weather Attribution (19 Sep 2023) claim: "Rain in eastern Libya is getting more extreme" -> Verdict: Partly backed.
  • Save the Children (3 Apr 2024) claim: "Zambia is drying out" -> Verdict: Partly opposite.
  • CSIRO and Bureau of Meteorology (Nov 2024) claim: "Northern Australia is getting wetter" -> Verdict: Partly opposite.
  • The New Humanitarian, quoting UN OCHA (19 Nov 2019) claim: "Droughts in Somalia are getting worse" -> Verdict: Depends where.

LIMITS The tool does not explain causes or make forecasts. A 25-year window is short for climate. Each study area is a 2° box, so local events can be missed. A verdict of "Not shown" means the data cannot separate a change from chance; it does not mean nothing changed.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES The frontend is built with Vite and plain JavaScript, using d3-geo for the globe and maps and topojson-client for geographical boundaries drawn from Natural Earth outlines (via the world-atlas package). Earlier versions used NASA Blue Marble and Black Marble imagery. Statistics were computed beforehand in Python using statsmodels. The platform is hosted as a static site on GitHub Pages.

USE OF AI

  • Claude (Anthropic) was used to design and write the product's code and interface, and to help with the analysis code.
  • Gemini (Google) was used to draft the submission text.
  • No AI is used inside the product: verdicts come from fixed statistical tests and a fixed vocabulary
